posts.title: Why we let oak rest for a year
posts.excerpt: Every board waits twelve months in the yard and another month by the bench before we cut it. Here is what the waiting does.
posts.content:
A board of white oak arrives at Joiner's Yard about as wet as a sponge you have wrung out by hand. If we made a table from it that week, the top would shrink across its width by the thickness of a pencil every winter, and split along the glue line by the second year.

Stickered, stacked and left alone

So the boards go on the rack under the long roof, each one lifted off the next by thin strips of wood called stickers, so the air can reach both faces. The rule is a year for every inch of thickness. Then they come inside and rest beside the bench for a month, to get used to a heated room.

You can hurry the cutting. You cannot hurry the wood.

Tomas Wren, tables and casework

Quarter-sawn boards, cut so the growth rings stand upright in the end grain, move about half as much as plain-sawn ones. They cost more and the sawmill gets fewer from each log. They are the reason our table tops stay flat in a centrally heated flat.

posts.title: The wedged tenon, drawn and explained
posts.excerpt: The dark marks on our chair legs and shelf sides are not decoration. They are wedges, and they are what holds the piece together.
posts.content:
Look at the side of the Open Shelf, or where the legs of the Oak Dining Chair meet the seat rail, and you will see small dark slivers of walnut in the pale oak. People often ask whether they are inlay. They are wedges, and they are doing the hardest work in the piece.

A tenon, a mortise, two wedges

  • The tenon is the tongue at the end of a rail.
  • The mortise is the rectangular hole it passes through, cut a little wider at the outside.
  • Two wedges are driven into saw cuts in the end of the tenon, spreading it like a dovetail inside the hole.

Once wedged, the tenon cannot be pulled out, glue or no glue. The joint gets tighter as the chair is sat on, and if one day it does loosen, it can be knocked apart, cleaned and wedged again.

A screw holds for ten years. A wedge holds for as long as the wood does.

Aiko Mori, chairmaker

posts.title: Re-oiling a table in twenty minutes
posts.excerpt: Water no longer beads on the top? A cloth, some hardwax oil and twenty minutes on a Sunday morning bring it back.
posts.content:
An oil finish lives in the top of the wood rather than on it. That is what makes it warm to the touch, and also why it needs feeding once or twice a year, more on a dining table than on a shelf.

What you need

  • A tin of clear hardwax oil (ours is in the care kit)
  • Two cotton cloths, old T-shirts are perfect
  • A sheet of 320-grit sandpaper for marks

Wipe the top with a damp cloth and let it dry. Sand any rings lightly along the grain. Rub in a thin coat, wait fifteen minutes, then wipe off everything that has not soaked in. Leave it overnight before the fruit bowl goes back on.

The full steps, with what to avoid, are on our care page. And if a mark will not move, bring it to Hal at the repair bench.

posts.title: A chair comes back after eleven years
posts.excerpt: Number 0042 left the workshop in 2015. This summer it came back with a loose back rail, three children's worth of dents and a story.
posts.content:
Every piece we make is signed and numbered under the seat. When chair 0042 came in this July, Aiko found its page in the old order book in two minutes: walnut rungs, oak seat, made for a family in Elmore Street in the spring of 2015.

Knocked apart, cleaned, wedged again

The back rail had worked loose, as rails do after a few thousand Sunday dinners. Hal knocked out the old wedges, cleaned the dried glue from the mortise, and drove in new walnut wedges. The dents were steamed out with a damp cloth and a hot iron, and the whole chair was oiled three times.

It came back looking like a chair that has been loved, which is the best kind.

Hal Ito, finishing and the repair bench

It went home a week later. The bill was $95, and the chair is good for another eleven years at least.

posts.title: The Long Bench now comes apart
posts.excerpt: After one too many narrow staircases, the Long Bench is now pegged instead of glued, and comes apart into four pieces for delivery.
posts.content:
Two metres of solid oak does not turn corners. After three deliveries this spring that ended with the bench going in through a window, Tomas redrew it.

Pegs instead of glue

The stretcher now meets the legs in drawbored joints: a peg through each tenon, slightly offset so it pulls the joint tight. Knock out four pegs and the bench comes apart into two leg frames, a stretcher and the top, small enough to carry up any staircase.

The new bench is on the showroom floor from this week. The price stays the same, and owners of the old glued version can have theirs converted at the repair bench.

products.name: Oak Dining Chair
products.short: A light dining chair in quarter-sawn white oak, the back rail keyed with walnut.
products.description:
Our first design, made since 2009 and still made by Aiko from start to finish. The seat is shaped by hand with a travisher so it fits without a cushion; the back rail is a single curved piece of oak, held by through-tenons locked with walnut keys.

Light enough to lift with one hand, strong enough for fifty years of dinners.

details.Size: W 46 × D 50 × H 79 cm, seat 45 cm

products.name: Cord Lounge Chair
products.short: A low walnut lounge chair with a seat and back woven from paper cord.
products.description:
A low, deep chair for reading, in solid black walnut. The frame is joined with bridle joints and pegs; the seat and back are woven by hand from about ninety metres of paper cord, which softens and darkens slowly with use.

The cord can be re-woven at our repair bench in a day.

details.Size: W 64 × D 78 × H 72 cm, seat 34 cm

products.name: Three-Leg Stool
products.short: A round oak stool on three turned legs, braced with thin walnut rungs.
products.description:
Three legs never rock, even on an old floor. The seat is cut from one piece of thick oak and gently dished; the legs are turned, then wedged right through the seat, and braced with walnut rungs.

Kitchen height or counter height: tell us in the order note.

products.name: Long Bench
products.short: A two-metre oak bench with a low walnut stretcher. Comes apart for delivery.
products.description: A plain long bench for a table, a hallway or the end of a bed. The top is a single quarter-sawn oak board; the legs meet the walnut stretcher in drawbored, pegged joints, so the bench comes apart into four pieces for narrow staircases.

details.Size: L 200 × D 34 × H 45 cm (or your length)

products.name: Low Table
products.short: A low oak table with splayed legs and walnut butterfly keys at the corners.
products.description: A low table for a sitting room or a tatami room. The top is two matched boards of quarter-sawn oak, the legs splay slightly outwards and are tenoned right through the top, then locked with walnut keys you can see at each corner.

products.name: Open Shelf
products.short: A four-shelf bookcase in white oak, the shelves wedged through the sides.
products.description: Four shelves, two sides and sixteen wedges. Every shelf passes right through the sides in a pair of tenons, locked with dark wedges on the outside; no back panel, no screws, no sag even under a row of art books.

products.name: Carved Walnut Tray
products.short: A tray carved from one piece of walnut, the gouge marks left on the inside.
products.description: Made from offcuts of the Lounge Chair walnut. Each tray is hollowed with a gouge and left with its tool marks inside, so no two are the same. For keys, bread, a pot of tea.

products.name: Wedged Tenon Study
products.short: A full-size wedged through-tenon in oak offcuts, for a desk or a shelf.
products.description: The joint that holds our chairs together, made as a small object from the offcuts. It comes apart: knock out the wedge, slide out the tenon, and see how it works. Apprentices make one in their first week.
